slo_title: Implement compile-time polymorphism in Java using method overloading.

mcq.q: Which of the following is NOT allowed in method overloading?
Which of the following best describes method overloading?

options.A: Defining the same method in different classes
options.B: Defining multiple methods with the same name but different parameters
options.C: Using the same class name in multiple packages

mcq.answer_text: Defining multiple methods with the same name but different parameters

mcq.q: What does the term "polymorphism" literally mean?
Which of the following implements compile-time polymorphism in Java?

options.C: It enables objects to behave differently based on context

mcq.answer_text: It enables objects to behave differently based on context

sq.q: Define polymorphism in Java and state its two main types.
answer: Polymorphism in Java refers to the ability of an object to take on many forms. The two main types are: Compile-time polymorphism (achieved through method overloading) Runtime polymorphism (achieved through method overriding)

sq.q: Write a simple Java class that demonstrates method overloading for calculating the area of a square and a rectangle.
answer: public class AreaCalculator { void area(int side) { System.out.println("Area of square: " + (side * side)); } void area(int length, int breadth) { System.out.println("Area of rectangle: " + (length * breadth)); } } Here, both area() methods have the same name but different parameter lists � this is compile-time polymorphism.

lq.q: You are developing a calculator tool. Users should be able to call a method calculate() to add: Two integers Two doubles Three integers Design a Java class using method overloading to support this. Explain how the JVM identifies which method to call. Discuss how compile-time polymorphism improves code clarity and flexibility.
answer: Java Code: public class Calculator { void calculate(int a, int b) { System.out.println("Sum (int): " + (a + b)); } void calculate(double a, double b) { System.out.println("Sum (double): " + (a + b)); } void calculate(int a, int b, int c) { System.out.println("Sum (3 ints): " + (a + b + c)); } public static void main(String[] args) { Calculator calc = new Calculator(); calc.calculate(5, 10); // Calls first method calc.calculate(5.5, 6.3); // Calls second method calc.calculate(1, 2, 3); // Calls third method } } JVM Method Resolution: The Java compiler determines which calculate() method to invoke at compile time, based on the number and type of arguments. This is why it's called compile-time polymorphism. Benefits: Code clarity: A single method name can perform logically similar operations without confusion. Ease of use: Users don�t need to remember multiple method names. Flexibility: The same method can handle various input types or conditions.
